extracted.intended_audience: general business and healthcare readers; investors, startup founders, regulators and journalists
extracted.subtask_description: A journalistic case study of the Theranos scandal focused on how leadership, culture, and investor/board dynamics allowed an allegedly unsafe, unvalidated medical product to reach the market. The piece draws lessons about startup governance, ethics, and the special responsibilities of medical technology companies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'fake it till you make it' for medical products
rubrics_metrics.description: Ms Holmes stands accused of applying Silicon Valley’s “fake it until you make it” mindset to medical care; releasing a “buggy” app in beta stage is one thing, but a medical product on which doctors and patients make life-and-death decisions must not be treated the same way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat clinical diagnostics like consumer software betas. Because some 70% of doctors’ decisions are based on blood tests, diagnostic devices must meet rigorous clinical standards and not be marketed or deployed until validated. Avoid rhetoric that normalizes premature roll-out of unvalidated medical technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure clinical validation and demonstrable accuracy before market roll-out
rubrics_metrics.description: The article states Theranos was allegedly nowhere near achieving her stated goals when its product was brought to market.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize thorough technical and clinical testing; require peer-reviewed or regulator-accepted evidence of accuracy and reliability before wide distribution. Market claims should be backed by independent validation and reproducible data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency with regulators, investors, partners, press and patients
rubrics_metrics.description: A culture of secrecy allegedly enabled a small inner circle to mislead and deceive Theranos staff, its board, investors, commercial partners, clients, members of the press and even federal regulators the FDA and CMS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Full, honest disclosure to regulators and stakeholders is required for trust and safety in healthcare. Avoid secrecy, selective disclosure, or deception; cooperate with oversight agencies and provide complete data when requested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Robust board oversight and distributed decision-making
rubrics_metrics.description: She took control of all decision-making. The board could not achieve quorum without her and non-disclosure agreements were used to silence former employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boards should be independent, technically competent or have access to relevant expertise, able to exercise meaningful oversight, and maintain quorum and governance processes that prevent single-person control. Avoid governance structures that concentrate unchecked authority in the founder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate an open culture that allows dissent and whistleblowing
rubrics_metrics.description: The corporate culture allegedly was dysfunctional: founded on fear, paranoia, secrecy and bullying; teams siloed and pitted against each other; dissent was punished with dismissal and NDAs used to silence employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foster psychological safety, channels for internal and external reporting, and protections for dissenting employees. Do not use NDAs or punitive measures to silence legitimate concerns about safety, ethics or accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not substitute charisma, image, or elite connections for technical merit
rubrics_metrics.description: Her single-minded drive, self-belief and brilliant sales pitch won champions in high places; she convinced prominent figures to join the board and investors to back the company despite lack of proven technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate technologies and founders on objective technical evidence and independent validation rather than charisma, uniform, celebrity endorsements, or high-profile backers. Investors, partners and board members should demand substantive proof of product claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage ethically with critics and the press; avoid suppression tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: When challenged, Ms Holmes and Mr Balwani allegedly surveilled, blackmailed, intimidated and litigated against critics; it is claimed she leaned on Rupert Murdoch to try to kill investigative reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respond to criticism through transparent disclosure and dialogue rather than intimidation or legal/extra-legal suppression. Ethical engagement with journalists, regulators and critics helps surface problems early and protects public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question cultural myths that elevate founders above scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: The article argues there is a Silicon Valley myth around founders—exemplified by Steve Jobs—that creates a culture of entitlement and magical thinking, which can lead to uncritical adulation of founders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investors, press and the public should apply critical scrutiny to founders’ claims and guard against mythologizing. Evaluate companies on measurable results and governance practices rather than founder legend or persona.
